target.text: No official target exists for this composite risk index - it's designed to identify relative risk, not track progress against a threshold. Lower scores indicate lower risk of digital exclusion.

source.name: Digital Exclusion Risk Index (DERI) v1.5 - Greater Manchester Combined Authority
source.notes: The GLA/LOTI 'Mapping Digital Exclusion' dataset previously cited as the intended source for this indicator is genuinely limited to its five pilot boroughs (Barnet, Brent, Kensington & Chelsea, Southwark, Westminster) - Lewisham isn't covered, and no Lewisham-specific output has been published from it, confirmed via the London Datastore and LOTI's own project pages. GMCA's Digital Exclusion Risk Index (DERI) does cover every LSOA in England, Scotland and Wales, so Ladywell's 7 constituent LSOAs (E01003273/274/275/276/278/279/291, confirmed via ONS's official LSOA-to-ward best-fit lookup) are all scored. 2.5 is the population-weighted average of those 7 LSOAs' individual DERI scores, using DERI's Great-Britain-normalised variant (England IMD basis) - the only one of DERI's three normalisation options (local authority / nation / Great Britain) that's comparable across different areas, per GMCA's own methodology guide. Scores range from 2.06 to 3.18 across the 7 LSOAs, i.e. genuine within-ward variation rather than a flat borough figure. Ladywell's score sits toward the low end of the 0-10 scale, consistent with Trust for London's own commentary that 'much of London, due to its relatively young demographic and good broadband access, is in the lower range' nationally. Caveat: DERI is a composite built from 11 proxy indicators (deprivation, demography, broadband access) across three domains, not a direct survey of who's actually offline, and several of its components are dated - 'no qualifications', 'social grade' and 'day-to-day activities limited' all come from Census 2011, while IMD is 2019-based and broadband/unemployment/pension-credit data is from 2019-2021. GMCA's in-progress v2.0 rebuild moves to 2021 Census data but has not yet published a scored output, and the repo's latest release (v1.6, November 2022) publishes no LSOA-level scores file, so v1.5 remains the latest version with usable LSOA scores. The previous indicator here - GLA's 2022 estimate of ~270,000 Londoners completely offline (London-wide, not Lewisham-specific) - is kept as descriptive context below rather than as the snapshot, since it measures something DERI doesn't (an absolute headcount rather than a relative risk score).

source.name: Lewisham Council: Main Grants Programme Allocations 2026-2029 (Mayor & Cabinet, 21 Jan 2026); Main Grants and Arts and Culture Grants Programme Allocations 2022-25 (Mayor & Cabinet, 2 Feb 2022)
source.notes: 2026-29 (current snapshot): there is no separate Arts and Culture Fund in the 2026-29 cycle. Following consultation, Mayor & Cabinet approved in July 2025 a model where arts and culture are funded within the Main Grants Programme's borough-wide capacity-building grants (report para 5.2.7, 5.2.9, 6.5), 'now delivered through a capacity-building lens rather than direct arts project funding' (para 3.3). Arts allocations recommended in the 21 January 2026 report (document s123458), per year: borough-wide arts grants £140,000 - The Albany / 2001 Company 'Creative Potential: Anchor Organisation Programme' £80,000, Lewisham Education Arts Network £30,000, Irie! dance theatre £20,000, Lewisham Music £10,000 - plus arts Transition grants £95,000 - Lewisham Youth Theatre, Second Wave and Midi Music £20,000 each, Entelechy Arts and Heart n Soul £15,000 each, Deptford X £5,000. Total £235,000 a year (£705,000 over three years), against the 2022-25 Arts and Culture Fund's £386,000 a year: a 39% cut, with The Albany's anchor grant down from £150,000 to £80,000. Transition grants exist to help previously funded organisations adapt to the new model (para 6.8-6.9). The whole programme totals £1,575,746 a year (para 1, recommendation 1). 2022-25 (previous snapshot): £386,000 is the ANNUAL general-fund budget of Lewisham's Arts and Culture Fund for 2022-25, not a 3-year total (corrected November 2026; it was previously labelled '£, 3-year total'). The Mayor & Cabinet report of 2 Feb 2022 (reattached as Appendix 1 to the March 2024 extension report, document s113598 - the lewisham.moderngov.co.uk copy returns a bot-check 403, the councilmeetings.lewisham.gov.uk mirror serves the same PDF) says the council's £1,836,308 core grants budget was split into '£1,450,308 for Main Grants and £386,000 for Arts and Culture' (para 1.4, 10.3), within a programme costed at '£2,459,308 per annum' including £623,000 Better Care Fund (para 4.3, 10.2). Recommended Arts & Culture grants (para 7.3.6; Appendix 2, document s113599, 'sub-total - Arts & Culture £387,000'): The Albany £150,000 (the fund's single large grant), plus ten smaller grants - Deptford X £20,000; Entelechy Arts, Irie!, Lewisham Education Arts Network, Lewisham Youth Theatre, Midi Music and Heart n Soul £30,000 each; Second Wave £28,750; Migration Museum £7,250; Montage Theatre Arts £1,000 (ten others, not eight; allocations total £387,000, £1,000 over the £386,000 budget). The fund was created by splitting the previous single Main Grants framework (agreed 14 Sept 2021, effective 1 April 2022), alongside an £800,000/year cut to the grants budget from 2022/23 (para 4.3, 10.2) while the council made 'at least £40m' of cuts over three years to April 2024 (para 4.3); existing arts grants were carried over 'with a proportionate cut' (para 4.7). The March 2024 extension report (s113597) extended the whole programme to 31 March 2026 at £2,329,308 (the 2022-25 total minus £130,000 of partnership grants), which implies the £386,000 arts budget continued in 2025/26, though the report doesn't itemise it. This is the council's dedicated arts grants stream only, not its total net arts/culture spend (MHCLG RO5 categories). National context, Equity news release 19 March 2026 (equity.org.uk/news/2026/cut-in-funding-by-british-councils-threatens-arts-access), reporting Autonomy Institute analysis behind the Equity Local Government Arts Funding Tracker: England 'council arts spending fell by 61%, with £660m less in real spending per year in 2024 compared with 2010. Current spending is a mere £6.47 per person, per year... down from £18.67'. Note the 61% is the fall in total real spending; the per-person fall (£18.67 to £6.47) is about 65%, so the two must not be paired as '61% (£18.67 to £6.47)'. Britain-wide (England, Scotland, Wales) the fall is 55%, £1.19bn to £539m in 2024-25 - the figure on the tracker page itself. Tracker methodology: net revenue outturn expenditure, CPI-adjusted to 2024-25 prices. The tracker (local-gov-arts-spending-tracker.apps.autonomy.work, a JavaScript app) also holds a Lewisham-specific 2010/11-2024/25 net arts spend series that could replace or supplement this snapshot with a real trend in future.

source.name: GLA London Datastore - Economic Fairness: Wealth Inequality
source.notes: No Lewisham- or borough-level wealth distribution figure exists (the underlying ONS Wealth and Assets Survey - WAS - is not designed to produce reliable local authority estimates), so this uses the GLA's London-wide figure instead, labelled accordingly: households in the bottom half of London's wealth distribution hold just 4% of the capital's total household wealth, while the richest 10% of households hold over 60%. Underlying source: ONS Wealth and Assets Survey microdata, as analysed by the GLA's Economic Fairness programme. An older Trust for London page (trustforlondon.org.uk/data/wealth-distribution/, now archived and no longer updated) put the same England-wide poorest-50%-wealth-share at 9% and London's bottom-half share at 6.8%, using 2018-2020 WAS data - the GLA's 4% figure is treated as the more current reference here, but the two aren't a clean like-for-like trend (different WAS rounds/methodology), so no trend array is given rather than implying a precise year-on-year decline. Caveat: the Office for Statistics Regulation removed WAS's Official Statistics accreditation in June 2025, saying it was 'no longer of sufficient value or quality to meet users' needs' - treat this figure as broadly indicative of London's wealth concentration, not a precise measurement. This session's WebFetch/curl tools were blocked for both trustforlondon.org.uk and ons.gov.uk, so the exact WAS survey round behind the GLA's 4% figure could not be independently confirmed.

source.notes: 7.22% of Lewisham residents aged 17+ had diabetes recorded on GP disease registers in 2024/25 (QOF prevalence), up from 5.67% in 2012/13.
